Top Takeaways for Clinicians from the
KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline
10 for the Management of Lupus Nephritis

Diagnosis of lupus nephritis Class III/IV ± V lupus nephritis
Early diagnosis and timely treatment of active lupus nephritis
are important to preserve nephrons. Changes in kidney function
1 or proteinuria based on serial measurements may suggest lupus Concomitant thrombotic Assess activity and
microangiopathy chronicity items
nephritis (LN), and this can be confirmed by kidney biopsy. (Section 10.3.1)
Active Class III/IV ± V Chronic Class III/IV ± V lupus nephritis
lupus nephritis without activity
Antimalarial therapy
Hydroxychloroquine is recommended for all patients with LN if
2 there are no contraindications. Supportive treatment If concomitant Class V
for chronic kidney disease manage as Class V
(Section 10.2.4)
Glucocorticoids
Methylprednisolone i.v. 0.25–0.50 g/d for 1–3 days as appropriate
Class I/II lupus nephritis depending on disease severity and rate of progression, then
prednisone p.o. at approximately 0.35–1.0 mg/kg/d
Immunosuppressive therapy in patients with Class I/II LN should (not to exceed 80 mg/d) and taper over a few months to
be guided by extrarenal disease manifestations unless the maintenance dose (the lower steroid dosing option referring
to the reduced-dose regimen in the voclosporin trials)†
patients have nephrotic syndrome due to lupus podocytopathy, (Practice Point 10.2.3.1.1)
3 which is managed as minimal change disease. and one of the
following options
Initial immunosuppression for active Class Mycophenolic acid Cyclophosphamide
III/IV lupus nephritis analogs (MPAA) for up to 6 months
for at least 6 months i.v. 500 mg q2wk × 6 or
The initial treatment of active proliferative (± membranous) LN is glucocorticoids plus MMF p.o. 1.0–1.5 g b.i.d. or 0.5–1.0 g/m2monthly × 6;
any one of the following: i. mycophenolic acid analogs (MPAA); ii. low-dose mycophenolic acid sodium or p.o. 1.0-1.5 mg/kg/d
0.72–1.08 g b.i.d. for 3 months
intravenous cyclophosphamide; iii. belimumab and either MPAA or low-dose (Practice Point 10.2.3.1.3) (Practice Point 10.2.3.1.2)§
intravenous cyclophosphamide; or iv. MPAA and a CNI when kidney function is not
4 CNI + MPAA Belimumab + MPAA or
severely impaired (i.e., eGFR ≤45 ml/min per 1.73 m2) (Figure 1)
Voclosporin 23.7 mg b.i.d. and MPAA in patients reduced-dose cyclophosphamide
with eGFR >45 ml/min per 1.73 m2 Belimumab (i.v., 10 mg/kg q2wk for
Glucocorticoid dosing Tacrolimus (trough level approximately 5.5 ng/ml 3 doses then q4wk) and MPAA or i.v.
[6.8 nmol/l], data mainly from Chinese patients) cyclophosphamide 500 mg q2wk × 6
<3.0 mg/dl (265 μmol/l) as initial and Belimumab duration up to 2.5 years
5 Although glucocorticoids have generally been given in high and reduced-dose MPAA in patients with SCr (Practice Point 10.2.3.1.5)
doses for LN, emerging data suggest that lower doses may be maintenance therapy
equally effective but with fewer short- and long-term toxicities. Consider cyclosporine when voclosporin
and tacrolimus are not available
(Practice Point 10.2.3.1.4)
CNI duration up to 3 years‡
Long-term immunosuppression for Class III/IV Figure 1
lupus nephritis
6 Following initial therapy of proliferative LN, MPAA is the
preferred immunosuppressive and should be continued for at
Reduce prednisone
least 36 months. (Figure 2) to <5 mg/d

triple immunosuppression or when azathioprine

active nephritis (refer to MPAA or available

7 pressure optimization, and hydroxychloroquine, and the
addition of immunosuppression in patients who develop 10.2.3.1.1 and Figure 5)
nephrotic range proteinuria.
Mycophenolic Continue with the Azathioprine CNI
or or or
acid analogs: maintenance triple 1.5–2.0 mg/kg/d (tacrolimus, level
Unsatisfactory response to treatment mycophenolate immunosuppression ≈4–6 ng/ml;
mofetil 1–2 g/d as described in Figure 5 cyclosporine, level
Unsatisfactory treatment responses can be due to non-adher- or as appropriate, Practice ≈50–100 ng/ml)
mycophenolic acid Point 10.2.3.2.5, and or mizoribine
720–1440 mg/d Figure 9 ≈3–5 mg/kg/d
chronic kidney damage that preclude complete resolution of
8 ence, inadequate immunosuppressant dosing, or significant or leflunomide
kidney abnormalities. Patients in whom these factors are ≈10–20 mg/d
Figure 2
excluded may have treatment-resistant LN. (Figure 3)
Verify adherence to treatment
End stage kidney disease 1
Ensure adequate dosing of immunosuppressive medications by measuring
plasma drug levels if applicable or available (check mycophenolic acid level
9 Kidney transplantation is the preferred form of kidney replace- 2
ment therapy for LN patients who develop end-stage kidney if on mycophenolic acid analogs/check infusion records if on cyclophosphamide)
disease.
Repeat biopsy if concern for chronicity or other diagnosis
3 (e.g., thrombotic microangiopathy)
Consider switching to an alternative recommended treatment regimen when
4 there is persistent active disease
Pregnancy in patients with lupus nephritis
Consider the following in patients refractory to first-line treatment regimens:
• Addition of rituximab or other biologic therapies
5 • Extended course of i.v. pulse cyclophosphamide
and planning. Pregnancy should be avoided when LN is active or
10 Good pregnancy outcomes require pre-pregnancy counselling • Enrollment in clinical trials if eligible
when patients are exposed to potentially teratogenic medica-
tions. Figure 3
